common_name: Perla Negra Maqui Berry (SAG-Registered Chilean Clonal Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings of this named clone in fertile, moisture-retentive soil; a male pollenizer plant is still needed since the species is dioecious.

directions: Perla Negra is one of three maqui clones selected and registered in 2015 with Chile's Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero by Universidad de Talca and Fundación Chile out of a wild-collection screening program begun in 2007, chosen for its large berries and unusually high polyphenol and anthocyanin content. It grows as a comparatively compact, well-behaved bush compared with wild maqui thickets, but it has little drought tolerance and needs steady moisture through fruit set. Expect only light bearing in the first couple of seasons after planting, with the clone reaching its characteristic heavy production from around the third growing season onward. Site it in southern Chile-type conditions with mild winters and cool, humid summers for best results.
sources: Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG) Chile — Registro de Variedades Protegidas

common_name: Luna Nueva Maqui Berry (SAG-Registered Chilean Clonal Selection)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained, humus-rich soil; pair with a male seedling or clone for pollination since maqui is dioecious.

directions: Luna Nueva is the earliest-ripening of the three maqui clones registered in 2015 by Universidad de Talca and Fundación Chile, flowering in early October in Chile's south-central growing zone and finishing its fruit by mid-December, well ahead of sister selections Morena and Perla Negra. The bush itself grows with notably lower vigor than wild maqui stands, staying smaller and more restrained, which makes it easier to manage in a cultivated row planting. Fruit size is medium, and the clone was chosen alongside the others for its strong anthocyanin content and reliable early yield. Give it a sheltered partial-shade to partial-sun spot with even moisture, since the species does not tolerate prolonged drought once established as a cultivated planting.
sources: Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG) Chile — Registro de Variedades Protegidas

common_name: Morena Maqui Berry (SAG-Registered Chilean Clonal Selection)

planting.note: Plant in full sun for best fruiting — this clone is more shade-sensitive than its sister selections — with a male pollenizer nearby.

directions: Morena is the latest-maturing of the three maqui clones registered in 2015 by Universidad de Talca and Fundación Chile, flowering in mid-October and finishing fruit around the end of December, and it carries medium-large berries with abundant foliage on a vigorous, leafy bush. It adapts well across different growing sites compared with its sister clones, but of the three it is the most sensitive to shade, producing noticeably less fruit when crowded or planted under cover, so it rewards a genuinely sunny position. Give it the room its vigorous habit demands and keep soil evenly moist through flowering and fruit set. As with all maqui, a male plant is needed nearby since the species is dioecious.
sources: Servicio Agrícola y Ganadero (SAG) Chile — Registro de Variedades Protegidas

planting.note: Plant seed tubers once soil is workable; hill as foliage grows.

directions: Camota is a distinctive native landrace of the Chiloé Archipelago, instantly recognizable by its variegated skin running from purple to near-black with bright yellow patches clustered around and between the eyes. Cut it open and the flesh itself is yellow, but purple pigment bleeds into the skin layer and part of the outer cortex and streaks inward from the vascular ring toward the center, giving slices a striking marbled look. Like its sister Chiloé landraces, it is maintained in small family plots rather than grown commercially, so plant whole or cut seed tubers in loose, fertile soil, hill as the vines grow, and keep moisture consistent through the cool, humid growing season typical of the archipelago. Harvest after the foliage dies back and cure tubers briefly before storing.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste — Chiloé potato documentation

common_name: Bruja Morada Potato (Purple Chiloé Heirloom Potato)

planting.note: Plant seed tubers once soil is workable; hill as foliage grows.

directions: Bruja Morada is a deep purple-skinned landrace from the Chiloé Archipelago's enormous reservoir of native potato diversity, one of several named 'bruja' types grown by Chilote smallholders. Its tubers hold notably high moisture content, which chefs and home cooks favor for salads and boiled preparations rather than frying, where a drier, starchier potato performs better. Grow it the way Chiloé growers traditionally have, planting whole or cut seed tubers in loose, humus-rich soil in a small mixed plot, hilling as stems emerge, and keeping moisture even through the archipelago's characteristically cool, wet growing season. Lift after vines die back and cure briefly in a cool, dark spot before storing.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste — Chiloé potato documentation

common_name: Pomme Gris Apple (Reinette Grise du Canada, Quebec Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil in full sun, with a compatible pollinizer nearby.

directions: Pomme Gris, also recorded as Reinette Grise du Canada, is one of the oldest named apples tied to Quebec, documented in Europe by the early 1800s and long believed to have either arrived with French or Swiss settlers or been selected in Canada itself and exported back across the Atlantic. The small-to-medium fruit develops a thick, suede-like russet coat over a yellow-green base, sometimes blushed rosy on the sun side, covering crisp, dense flesh with a rich, nutty sweetness and notes of cider and pear. Unlike many old Quebec apples bred for fresh eating alone, Pomme Gris is prized as a long-keeping winter apple that holds its quality in storage for months, and it also makes excellent cider. Plant it on hardy rootstock suited to short, cold Quebec-style seasons and give it a pollinizer, since it is not self-fertile.

common_name: Thibodeau de Comte Beauce Bean (Beauce County Quebec Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct-sow once soil has warmed; this bush bean dries down unusually fast even in a cool, short Quebec-style season.

directions: Thibodeau de Comte Beauce is a rare, very productive bush bean from Beauce County, Quebec, with rosy-pink flowers giving way to straight green pods splashed and streaked with purple-red, and white seeds marked with maroon stripes and spots. Some seed stewards trace its cultivation back to the St. Lawrence Iroquois, and it has long been kept going mainly through small-scale home gardeners rather than commercial seed trade. It is notably quick to dry down on the vine even in cool, damp conditions that slow other dry beans, making it a dependable choice for short-season gardens. Pick pods young and tender for snap use, or let them mature fully for a productive dry shell bean good in baked beans and soups.

common_name: Heritage Dore Bean (Cantin Family Quebec Heirloom)

planting.note: Direct-sow as a bush dry bean once soil has warmed past frost danger.

directions: Heritage Dore was grown for generations in the family garden of the Cantin family in Portneuf County, Quebec, before being retrieved and shared more broadly as a French-Canadian heirloom dry bean. The oval seeds are glossy beige to light mustard-gold with a distinctive white eye ringed in brown, each about two-thirds of an inch long, and the bush plants dry down reliably for a full crop of storage beans. It is traditionally used in Quebec-style baked beans, where its mild, slightly sweet flavor and good texture after slow cooking are especially valued. Grow it as a standard bush bean, direct-sown after frost danger passes, watered evenly through flowering and pod fill, and left to dry fully on the plant before harvest.

common_name: Gourgane Petite du Lac (Lac-Saint-Jean Heirloom Fava Bean)

planting.note: Direct-sow as soon as soil can be worked in earliest spring; this small-seeded fava thrives in the cool summers where common beans struggle.

directions: Known in Quebec as gourgane, this small-seeded fava bean descends from broad beans brought over by the earliest French settlers and has remained a staple of the Lac-Saint-Jean and Charlevoix regions, where summers are cool enough that common beans are a chancy crop but fava beans thrive. The Petite du Lac strain was preserved within one Lac-Saint-Jean family's seed stock and later shared more widely by regional seed savers after decades of being maintained only at home-garden scale. It is the bean behind soupe aux gourganes, a classic regional dish built around the small, tender-skinned seeds simmered into a hearty vegetable soup. Sow directly into cool soil weeks before the last frost, since mature plants shrug off light frost, and harvest pods young for fresh shelling or let them dry fully for soup beans.
